anchors.fact: Jules and Mme Verne sent "a special letter" asking her to stop and see them, if she could. She thought she'd have to decline (Bly, ch. III; card F2). Why they asked isn't on the page (I1; audit X7).
anchors.meaning: I like to think they wanted nothing but your company. (Our reading, signposted.)

anchors.fact: Her promise was public: seventy-five days (ch. IV; F10).
anchors.meaning: You make the promise first, and where everyone can see.

anchors.fact: It could be done only by going without sleep and rest for two nights. Once she knew she'd miss no connection, she said not to think about it (ch. III; F3; audit X2).
anchors.meaning: The distance has never frightened you.

anchors.fact: Her own record: 179½ miles out of her way, the hours starred in her table (ch. XVIII; F13).
anchors.meaning: You count the cost and go anyway.

anchors.fact: It hung on a special mail train ("that will not give us time to see Verne"), and at Amiens they were locked in the carriage and feared being carried past (ch. III; F4–F5). **The mail train is dossier only** (cut from y2, Robin 2026-10-06, F3); the locked carriage stays in y2.
anchors.meaning: Up to the last second, it might have come to nothing.

anchors.fact: On the platform, she wondered "if my face was travel-stained, and if my hair was tossed" (ch. IV; F7).
anchors.meaning: It was never the distance. It's the second before you see their face.

anchors.fact: They "stood on the platform waiting our arrival", and the welcome made her forget how untidy she was. Indoors, Mme Verne lit the fire with her own hands (ch. IV; F6, F8, F17).
anchors.meaning: They weren't waiting for a rescue. They were waiting for you.

anchors.fact: "Contrary to his regular rules", Verne took a glass of wine to drink to her success. Glasses clinked; "Good luck, Nellie Bly" (ch. IV; F9–F10). y4 now says he "raised a glass of wine to her success" (F3 cut, 2026-10-06); the "wine and biscuit" and the clinking glasses are dossier only.
anchors.meaning: Someone broke his own rule to raise a glass to you.

anchors.fact: He'd applaud with both hands at seventy-nine days, and she knew he doubted her seventy-five (ch. IV; F10).
anchors.meaning: Being loved isn't the same as being believed. They wished you well anyway.

anchors.fact: Bareheaded, they followed her into the cold courtyard and waved from the gate (ch. IV; F11).
anchors.meaning: The cold was real. So was the warmth that came out into it.

anchors.fact: She feared the visit had "jeopardized the success of my tour" (ch. V; F12).
anchors.meaning: The doubt on the way back, never about the journey.

anchors.fact: She finished in 72 days. The Vernes' cable was to reach her "the moment she touches American soil", and at Jersey City she cheered because she was "home again" (chs. XVII–XVIII; F14–F16).
anchors.meaning: You kept it, and they had kept you in mind the whole way.

anchors.fact: A whisky sour with a float of red wine is a drink of the 1880s, first attested in Chicago in 1883. In saloon talk any red wine was "claret". New York Sour is the name that lasted (Oxford pdf 1387; *Imbibe!* pdf 96; NY Sour card F1–F4). **Dossier only** (cut from y4, Robin 2026-10-06, F3); the rye's reason stays in Checks › Pairings.
anchors.meaning: Whiskey and red wine already belonged together in her decade (audit Y1: never "rye and red wine" for the 1880s). Never "her drink".

anchors.fact: Until the 1840s, when New Yorkers began icing them, Cock-Tails were "drunk at room temperature" (Oxford pdf 1049; audit D3).
anchors.meaning: Warm the old way: the warmth was people, and nothing in the glass is cold. (Our reading.)

cocktail.closingLine: Raise it to someone first. When one's raised to you, you've brought enough.
cocktail.glassware: stemmed red wine glass (about 250 ml), at room temperature, no ice
method: Keep everything out of the fridge: the rye, the wine, the water and the glass all stay at room temperature. A cool room is best. No ice, at any point.
Pour the syrup, the bitters and the rye into the glass and stir for a few seconds to mix.
Add the wine and the water, then stir gently three or four times.
Hold the orange peel over the glass, skin side down, and squeeze it so its oils fall on the drink. Set the peel aside, so nothing is in the glass when it's raised.
cocktail.name: Out of Your Way

recipe.note: "Claret" is the old English name for red Bordeaux. Any dry, medium-bodied red works if it isn't oaky or sweet. The story names no wine, so this one is my choice.
1½ teaspoons: equal weights of demerara sugar and warm water, stirred until dissolved, then cooled. Use up to 10 ml if your wine is firm and grippy.
at room temperature, not from the fridge
squeezed over the top, then set aside

cocktail.tagline: Some people send their love. You bring it.

reading.epigraph: This cocktail is made at room temperature. Some things shouldn't arrive cold.
whoYouAre: Someone you love says it's a shame you can't make it. It's three hundred miles away, in the middle of the week. You don't argue. On the night, you're there, on time, in your good coat, and the whole room turns round. That's how you love. Not a card, not a call. You said you'd come, so you come, the whole way, with everyone watching. Anyone you love never has to wonder whether you'll be there, and everyone around them can see how loved they are. Nobody forgets being loved like that.

It was never the distance. It's the second before you see their face, when you don't know yet whether they're glad you came, or whether they'd have been fine without you. You'd never admit it, but somewhere along the way, being needed started to feel like the proof that you're loved. It isn't the only proof. Most of the time, it isn't even the best one.
yours: In November 1889, a reporter called Nellie Bly set out to go round the world faster than the hero of Jules Verne's novel, who took eighty days. She had promised seventy-five. When her ship reached England, she heard that Verne and his wife had written to ask her to visit them at home in Amiens. It was out of her way, and she'd assumed she would have to say no. It would mean two nights without sleep. If she missed no connections, she said, "don't think about sleep or rest."

It nearly came to nothing: at Amiens they were locked in their compartment and thought they'd be carried past. Then she stepped onto the platform, and the Vernes were standing there, waiting for her. What she wrote about that moment isn't the miles or the lost sleep: "I wondered if my face was travel-stained, and if my hair was tossed." A second later, she wrote, the welcome had made her forget all about it.

That's the second I mean. You'd make the whole journey without a thought and still feel it on the platform. And look at who was waiting. I like to think they wanted nothing but her company. When it was time to go, they came out into the cold courtyard without hats and stood at the gate waving, the wind blowing their white hair about. Nobody there was worried about anyone's hair.

Before she left, Verne, against his own rules, raised a glass of wine to her success and managed the toast in English, for her: "Good luck, Nellie Bly." Her book never says what the wine was, so the wine in the cocktail I've made for you is my choice: a young red Bordeaux, and it's more than half the drink, because the toast was the wine. With it goes straight rye. Then a little dark sugar syrup, Angostura bitters, a splash of water, and the scent of orange peel. Ice never comes near it. It's made and served at room temperature, soft, deep and warming: a good red with a spine of rye. I made it warm for the fire Verne's wife lit with her own hands when they arrived, and for the two of them standing bareheaded in the cold courtyard to wave her off.

So go and see someone who's doing perfectly well without you. No occasion, nothing to fix, nobody to rescue: just because you'd like to see them. You'll feel that second at the door, the same as always. Let it come. When their face lights up, it won't be for anything you've done. That's what being wanted looks like, and you've had it all along.
